events/churches-of-christ-census-1906/ti: U.S. Religious Census lists the Churches of Christ separately
events/churches-of-christ-census-1906/su: At the request of David Lipscomb, editor of the Gospel Advocate, the 1906 U.S. Census of Religious Bodies listed the 'Churches of Christ' separately from the 'Disciples of Christ', formally recognising a division in the Stone-Campbell movement that had been widening for decades, largely along Northern/Southern and urban/rural lines.
events/churches-of-christ-census-1906/ca: Dispute over instrumental music in worship and missionary societies
Different readings of the silence of Scripture (what the New Testament does not authorise)
Post–Civil War sectional and economic divides
events/churches-of-christ-census-1906/co: Churches of Christ (a cappella) as a distinct fellowship
Disciples and the later independent Christian Churches developed separately
events/pyongyang-great-revival-1907/summ: During a Bible class at Jangdaehyun Church in January 1907, Korean elder Kil Seon-ju and others led public confession of sins that spread through the Presbyterian and Methodist churches. Early-morning prayer and Bible study became hallmarks of Korean Protestantism; Pyongyang was called the 'Jerusalem of the East'.
events/pilot-point-union-1908/title: Holiness union at Pilot Point forms the Church of the Nazarene
events/pilot-point-union-1908/summary: In October 1908 the Pentecostal Church of the Nazarene — itself the 1907 union of Phineas Bresee's Los Angeles Church of the Nazarene (1895) and the eastern Association of Pentecostal Churches of America — joined with the southern Holiness Church of Christ at Pilot Point, Texas. Nazarenes count this as their founding; 'Pentecostal' was dropped from the name in 1919 to avoid confusion with the tongues movement.
events/pilot-point-union-1908/causes/0: Holiness believers leaving or expelled from Methodism over entire sanctification
events/pilot-point-union-1908/causes/1: Desire to unite regional holiness bodies into a national church
events/pilot-point-union-1908/consequenc: Largest denomination of the Wesleyan-Holiness tradition
Distinguished itself from Pentecostalism by rejecting tongues as the evidence of Spirit baptism
events/scofield-reference-bible-1909/sum: Cyrus I. Scofield's annotated King James Bible built Darby's dispensational premillennialism into its notes, dividing history into seven dispensations and distinguishing Israel and the church. It sold millions and shaped fundamentalist and evangelical eschatology for generations.
events/edinburgh-missionary-conference-1: Some 1,200 delegates of Protestant mission societies, chaired by John R. Mott, met to plan 'the evangelisation of the world in this generation'. Only about 18 delegates were from Asia; V. S. Azariah's plea 'give us friends' became famous. Its continuation committee led to the International Missionary Council and the ecumenical movement.
events/the-fundamentals-1910/summary: Funded by oil businessmen Lyman and Milton Stewart, ninety essays in twelve volumes defended biblical inerrancy, the virgin birth, substitutionary atonement, bodily resurrection and miracles against higher criticism and liberal theology. Distributed free to clergy, they gave the name 'fundamentalist' to the movement.
events/assembleia-de-deus-belem-1911/tit: Swedish missionaries found the Assembleia de Deus in Belém
events/assembleia-de-deus-belem-1911/sum: Daniel Berg and Gunnar Vingren, Swedish Baptists who had received Spirit baptism in Chicago, arrived in Belém in 1910. Expelled from the local Baptist church with eighteen followers in June 1911, they formed the Apostolic Faith Mission, renamed the Assembleia de Deus in 1918.
events/assembleia-de-deus-belem-1911/cau: Influence of William Durham's Chicago revival
Prophecy directing Berg and Vingren to Pará
events/assembleia-de-deus-belem-1911/con: Grew into Brazil's largest Protestant family and one of the largest Pentecostal movements in the world
Fragmented into many conventions and ministries (CGADB, CONAMAD and others)
events/malankara-catholicate-1912/title: Catholicate established in Malankara; Orthodox–Jacobite division
events/malankara-catholicate-1912/summar: After Patriarch Abdullah II of the Syriac Orthodox Church excommunicated Metropolitan Vattasseril Geevarghese Mar Dionysius (1911), his party invited the earlier-deposed Patriarch Abdul Masih II, who consecrated a Catholicos for the East in Malankara in 1912. The church divided between those who stressed Malankara autonomy (later the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church) and those who stressed obedience to the Patriarch of Antioch (the Jacobite Syrian Christian Church).
events/malankara-catholicate-1912/causes: Disputes over control of church property and the authority of the Antiochene patriarch in India
Indian Christian self-assertion under colonial rule
events/malankara-catholicate-1912/conseq: Two parties ('Methran' and 'Bava' factions) and decades of litigation
Reunion in 1958 after a Supreme Court of India ruling; renewed division from 1975
Supreme Court judgement of 2017 holding the 1934 constitution binding on parishes, followed by disputes over church buildings
events/harris-movement-west-africa-1913/: The Liberian Grebo prophet William Wade Harris, in white robe with cross, Bible and calabash, walked along the Ivory Coast and Gold Coast calling people to burn fetishes and be baptised. Perhaps 100,000–120,000 people converted in eighteen months before French authorities expelled him; Methodist and Harrist churches grew from his work.
Harris's prison vision of the angel Gabriel
events/oneness-new-issue-1913/title: The 'New Issue': baptism in Jesus' name at the Arroyo Seco camp meeting
events/oneness-new-issue-1913/summary: At the Worldwide Apostolic Faith camp meeting at Arroyo Seco near Los Angeles in April 1913, R. E. McAlister remarked that the apostles baptised in the name of Jesus only. Frank Ewart and Glenn Cook began rebaptising believers in Jesus' name in 1914, teaching that Jesus is the name of the one God. In 1916 the Assemblies of God adopted a Trinitarian Statement of Fundamental Truths and about a quarter of its ministers left.
events/oneness-new-issue-1913/causes/0: Restorationist reading of Acts 2:38 and the 'finished work' teaching of William Durham
events/oneness-new-issue-1913/consequenc: Origin of Oneness (Apostolic) Pentecostalism, outside historic Nicene Trinitarianism
Formation of the Pentecostal Assemblies of the World and later the United Pentecostal Church International
events/iglesia-ni-cristo-registered-1914: Felix Manalo registers the Iglesia ni Cristo

On 27 July 1914 Felix Y. Manalo, who had passed through Methodist, Presbyterian, Christian Mission (Disciples) and Seventh-day Adventist churches, registered the Iglesia ni Cristo with the American colonial government. Its members regard Manalo as God's last messenger, the 'angel from the east' of Revelation 7:2, re-establishing the true church in the Philippines.
Manalo's study of Scripture and conclusion that the church had apostatised
Nationalist sentiment under American colonial rule
Became one of the largest indigenous churches in Asia, with bloc-voting influence in Philippine politics
Leadership passed to Eraño Manalo (1963) and Eduardo Manalo (2009)
events/armenian-genocide-1915/summary: During World War I the Ottoman government deported and massacred an estimated one million or more Armenians, along with Syriac (Assyrian) Christians in the Sayfo ('sword') and Greeks of Anatolia. Death marches ended in the Syrian desert at Deir ez-Zor. The ancient Christian presence in Anatolia was nearly erased.
events/armenian-genocide-1915/causes/0: Ottoman wartime nationalism and fear of Christian minorities
events/armenian-genocide-1915/consequenc: Canonisation of the martyrs by the Armenian Church (2015)
events/fatima-apparitions-1917/summary: Three shepherd children — Lúcia, Francisco and Jacinta — reported six appearances of the Virgin Mary between May and October 1917, calling for prayer, penance and the consecration of Russia. On 13 October a crowd reported the 'miracle of the sun'. The church approved the devotion in 1930.
events/fatima-apparitions-1917/causes/0: Wartime anxieties and Portuguese anticlerical republic
events/moscow-council-and-revolution-191: Moscow Council restores the patriarchate; Bolshevik persecution begins

The All-Russian Church Council restored the patriarchate and elected Tikhon in November 1917, days after the Bolshevik revolution. The Soviet state separated church and state, confiscated property and launched persecutions that killed tens of thousands of clergy and believers in the following decades.
Catacomb church and Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia
events/watch-tower-schism-1917/title: Bible Students divide after the death of Charles Taze Russell
events/watch-tower-schism-1917/summary: After Russell died in October 1916, Joseph F. Rutherford became president of the Watch Tower Society in January 1917. His removal of four directors and the publication of The Finished Mystery that year divided the Bible Students. Many who remained loyal to Russell's writings formed independent fellowships such as the Pastoral Bible Institute (1918) and the Dawn Bible Students; those who stayed with the Society took the name Jehovah's witnesses in 1931.
events/watch-tower-schism-1917/causes/0: Disputed succession and Rutherford's centralisation of authority
events/watch-tower-schism-1917/causes/1: Disagreement over whether Russell's Studies in the Scriptures were final
events/watch-tower-schism-1917/consequen: Separate history of Independent Bible Students
Rutherford-era doctrinal and organisational changes in what became Jehovah's Witnesses
events/russian-church-abroad-1920/title: Russian Church Abroad organised in exile
events/russian-church-abroad-1920/summar: Russian bishops evacuated with the White armies formed a Supreme Church Administration Abroad in Constantinople (November 1920), citing Patriarch Tikhon's decree no. 362 permitting dioceses cut off from Moscow to govern themselves. In 1921 it moved to Sremski Karlovci in Serbia, where an all-diaspora council met.
events/russian-church-abroad-1920/longTe: The Synod moved from Sremski Karlovci (Serbia) to Munich after the Second World War and to New York in 1950. Its relationship with Moscow was broken for most of the Soviet period; it canonised the New Martyrs of Russia in 1981. On 17 May 2007, Metropolitan Laurus and Patriarch Alexy II signed the Act of Canonical Communion, making ROCOR a self-governing part of the Moscow Patriarchate; a minority of clergy and parishes refused the union.
events/russian-church-abroad-1920/causes: Russian Civil War and emigration of over a million Russians
Bolshevik persecution and the isolation of Patriarch Tikhon
events/russian-church-abroad-1920/conseq: Formation of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia (ROCOR)
Rejection of Metropolitan Sergius's 1927 declaration of loyalty to the Soviet state
Act of Canonical Communion with the Moscow Patriarchate (2007)
events/kimbanguist-movement-1921/summary: Simon Kimbangu, a Baptist catechist in the Belgian Congo, began a healing and preaching ministry at Nkamba in April 1921 that drew crowds and emptied mission churches. Arrested within months and sentenced to death (commuted), he spent thirty years in prison; his followers formed one of Africa's largest independent churches.
events/kimbanguist-movement-1921/causes/: Bible-reading Baptist converts seeking African prophecy
events/kimbanguist-movement-1921/consequ: Kimbanguist Church (EJCSK), member of WCC since 1969
